claim: The decline of sequence and structural similarities between ancient protein orthologs with conserved molecular function significantly slows down after ~1–2 billion years of independent evolution.
source: Our results demonstrate that the decline of sequence and structural similarities between such orthologs significantly slows down after ~1–2 billion years of independent evolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and computational analysis of protein sequence and structural divergence patterns across evolutionary time, as shown in multiple figures throughout the manuscript.

claim: The sequence and structural similarities between ancient orthologs have not substantially decreased for the past billion years.
source: As a result, the sequence and structural similarities between ancient orthologs have not substantially decreased for the past billion years.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of divergence patterns showing saturation of sequence and structural divergence at long evolutionary timescales.

claim: The effective divergence limit is greater than 25% sequence identity between ancient orthologs.
source: The effective divergence limit (>25% sequence identity) is not primarily due to protein sites universally conserved in all linages.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting to sequence divergence data across multiple enzyme families, as shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Less than four amino acid types are accepted, on average, per site across orthologous protein sequences that maintain the same molecular function.
source: Instead, less than four amino acid types are accepted, on average, per site across orthologous protein sequences.
evidence: This claim is derived from the Y0 parameter in Model 2, which represents the inverse of the average number of acceptable amino acid types per site.

claim: Protein sites with experimentally determined small and large fitness effects of mutations show different divergence patterns.
source: Our analysis also reveals different divergence patterns for protein sites with experimentally determined small and large fitness effects of mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental MAGE data for FolA and InfA proteins showing distinct temporal divergence patterns for sites grouped by fitness effects.

claim: Proteins with the same structural fold frequently diverge to very low (~10%) levels of sequence identity.
source: It was previously demonstrated that proteins with the same structural fold frequently diverge to very low (~10%) levels of sequence identity (Rost, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Rost, 1997.

claim: Conservation of protein fold exerts relatively minor constraints on how far protein sequences can diverge.
source: These results suggest that conservation of protein fold, that is, the overall arrangement and topological connections of protein secondary structures (Murzin et al., 1995), exerts relatively minor constraints on how far protein sequences can diverge.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that proteins with the same fold can diverge to very low sequence identity, combined with established knowledge about protein folds.

claim: Only a relatively small fraction of protein residues (~3–5%) are usually directly involved in catalysis.
source: While only a relatively small fraction of protein residues (~3–5%) are usually directly involved in catalysis (Lehninger et al., 2013), recent analyses have demonstrated that even sites located far from catalytic residues may be significantly constrained in evolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lehninger et al., 2013, representing established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Sites located far from catalytic residues may be significantly constrained in evolution because substitutions at these sites can have substantial effects on molecular function.
source: While only a relatively small fraction of protein residues (~3–5%) are usually directly involved in catalysis (Lehninger et al., 2013), recent analyses have demonstrated that even sites located far from catalytic residues may be significantly constrained in evolution. Because substitutions at these sites can have substantial effects on molecular function (Firnberg et al., 2016), it is likely that functionally-related sequence constraints extend far beyond catalytic residues.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Firnberg et al., 2016, and represents an inference about the extent of functional constraints.

claim: The Enzyme Commission (EC) classifies enzymatic functions using a hierarchical 4-digit code such that two enzymes that share all four EC digits catalyze the same biochemical reaction.
source: The Enzyme Commission (EC) classifies enzymatic functions using a hierarchical 4-digit code (Bairoch, 1999), such that two enzymes that share all four EC digits catalyze the same biochemical reaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bairoch, 1999, and represents established knowledge about enzyme classification.

claim: Protein sequences representing 64 EC numbers from 22 diverse model organisms across the three domains of life were used in the analysis.
source: We used protein sequences representing 64 EC numbers from 22 diverse model organisms across the three domains of life (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim describes the data used in the study.

claim: The considered enzymatic activities include members of all six major enzyme classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases and ligases.
source: The considered activities include members of all six major enzyme classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases and ligases.
evidence: This claim describes the scope of enzymatic activities analyzed in the study.

claim: In 62 of the 64 cases, Model 2 (with a divergence limit) fits the sequence divergence data significantly better than Model 1 (without a divergence limit).
source: In 62 of the 64 cases, the second model fits the divergence data significantly better than the first model (F-test p-value<0.05, Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test) of model fits to sequence divergence data.

claim: In 95% of the cases (61/64) the maximum likelihood value of the parameter Y0 is significantly higher than the average sequence identity between random protein sequences (~13.5%).
source: Moreover, in 95% of the cases (61/64) the maximum likelihood value of the parameter Y0 is significantly higher (Wald test p-value<0.05) than the average sequence identity between random protein sequences based on their optimal global alignment (~13.5%, shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 by dashed black lines).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wald test) and comparison to baseline sequence identity shown in figures.

claim: The distribution of the fitted parameter Y0 suggests a long-term sequence identity >25% (with average ~40%) between considered orthologs.
source: The distribution of the fitted parameter Y0 suggests a long-term sequence identity >25% (with average ~40%) between considered orthologs (Figure 2a); this demonstrates that conservation of a specific enzymatic function significantly limits long-term protein sequence divergence.
evidence: This claim is supported by the distribution of Y0 values shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Conservation of a specific enzymatic function significantly limits long-term protein sequence divergence.
source: The distribution of the fitted parameter Y0 suggests a long-term sequence identity >25% (with average ~40%) between considered orthologs (Figure 2a); this demonstrates that conservation of a specific enzymatic function significantly limits long-term protein sequence divergence.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the Y0 parameter distribution showing high long-term sequence identity.

claim: Model 2 is mathematically equivalent to a divergence model with equal substitution rates across sites, a limited number of amino acid types accepted per site, and allowed back substitutions.
source: Notably, model two is mathematically equivalent (see Materials and methods) to a divergence model with equal substitution rates across sites, a limited number of amino acid types accepted per site, and allowed back substitutions (Tajima and Nei, 1984; Gilson et al., 2017; Yang, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical derivation in Materials and methods and citations to previous work.

claim: In Model 2, the parameter Y0 represents the inverse of the effective number of acceptable amino acid types per site during protein evolution.
source: In this model, the parameter Y0 represents the inverse of the effective number of acceptable amino acid types per site during protein evolution.
evidence: This claim is based on the mathematical equivalence of Model 2 to a model with limited amino acid types per site.

claim: On average, only 2 to 4 amino acids are acceptable per site for proteins that strictly conserve their molecular function.
source: Our results thus suggest that, on average, only 2 to 4 amino acids are acceptable per site for proteins that strictly conserve their molecular function (Figure 2a, top blue X axis); we note that this low average number does not contradict the fact that more than four amino acid types could be observed at a given protein site at low frequencies (Breen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is derived from the Y0 parameter values and their interpretation as the inverse of acceptable amino acid types.

claim: The rates of protein sequence divergence between orthologous enzymes have decreased by more than 10 times during ~4 billion years of evolution according to Model 3 fits.
source: The best fits of such a variable-rate model (blue in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showed that the rates of protein sequence divergence between orthologous enzymes have decreased by more than 10 times during ~4 billion years of evolution (see Materials and methods and Supplementary file 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by fitting Model 3 (gamma distribution of substitution rates) to the sequence divergence data.

claim: The vast majority of orthologous enzymes with the same function will remain above 25% sequence identity on the timescales when Earth environments will be hospitable to life (1–3 billion years from the present).
source: Although the third model does not explicitly consider a long-term divergence limit, the obtained model fits also show that the vast majority of orthologous enzymes with the same function will remain above 25% sequence identity on the timescales when Earth environments will be hospitable to life (1–3 billion years from the present O'Malley-James et al., 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on projections from Model 3 fits and citation to O'Malley-James et al., 2014 for Earth habitability timescales.

claim: The observed divergence limit is not an artifact due to difficulty detecting remote protein homologs, as it occurs at relatively high sequence identities.
source: The observed divergence limit is not an artifact due to difficulty detecting remote protein homologs, as it occurs at relatively high sequence identities (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), for which corresponding orthologs can be easily identified by computational sequence comparison methods.
evidence: This claim addresses a potential methodological concern by noting that the divergence limit occurs at sequence identities well above detection thresholds.

claim: The results remain similar when restricted to orthologous enzyme pairs with experimentally validated molecular functions.
source: Furthermore, the results remained similar when we restricted the analysis to orthologous enzyme pairs with experimentally validated molecular functions (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), based on publications referenced in the BRENDA database (Chang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by additional analysis using only experimentally validated enzyme functions.

claim: The results remain robust towards the variance in the estimates of divergence times between considered species.
source: The results also remain robust towards the variance in the estimates of divergence times between considered species (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis described in Materials and methods.

claim: The divergence limit is reached when, due to a small number of amino acids types accepted per protein site and back substitutions, additional amino acid replacements do not lead to a substantial further increase in protein sequence and structural divergence.
source: Instead, the effective limit is reached when, due to a small number of amino acids types accepted per protein site and back substitutions, additional amino acid replacements do not lead to a substantial further increase in protein sequence and structural divergence (Meyer et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim provides a mechanistic explanation for the divergence limit, supported by citation to Meyer et al., 1986.

claim: The divergence rate between protein orthologs drops, on average, to only ~2% sequence identity decrease per billion years when their mutual sequence identity reaches 30%.
source: For example, the divergence rate between protein orthologs drops, on average, to only ~2% sequene identity decrease per billion years when their mutual sequence identity reaches 30% (corresponding to protein distance of 70%; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by calculation of divergence rates from Model 3 fits, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Model 2 fitted the data significantly better than Model 1 for the majority (23/29) of non-enzymatic protein families, and the parameter Y0 was >25% for these families.
source: Based on the same set of 22 species used in the analysis of enzyme families, we found that model two fitted the data significantly better than model one, and that the parameter Y0 was >25% for the majority (23/29) of the non-enzymatic protein families (Figure 2b, Supplementary file 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of model fits for non-enzymatic proteins.

claim: 19 additional orthologous groups showed two clearly different divergence patterns, with pairs of eukaryotic orthologs diverging substantially faster and farther than prokaryotic orthologs in the same protein family.
source: Interestingly, we also identified 19 additional orthologous groups showing two clearly different divergence patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 6), with pairs of eukaryotic orthologs diverging substantially faster and farther than prokaryotic orthologs in the same protein family.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of divergence patterns shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The orthologous groups with different divergence patterns between eukaryotic and prokaryotic orthologs included mitochondrial ribosomal proteins and initiation factors of mitochondrial translation.
source: The orthologous groups with this behavior included mitochondrial ribosomal proteins and initiation factors of mitochondrial translation (Supplementary file 2e).
evidence: This claim identifies specific protein families showing differential divergence patterns.

claim: Mitochondrial ribosomal proteins diverged significantly faster in eukaryotes, compared to the divergence between their bacterial orthologs, due to compensatory protein substitutions following the accumulation of slightly deleterious substitutions in the mitochondrial ribosomal RNA.
source: It has been previously postulated that mitochondrial ribosomal proteins diverged significantly faster in eukaryotes, compared to the divergence between their bacterial orthologs, due to compensatory protein substitutions following the accumulation of slightly deleterious substitutions in the mitochondrial ribosomal RNA (Barreto and Burton, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Barreto and Burton, 2013.

claim: Only a relatively small fraction of protein sites (10–20%) are universally conserved, that is, they are identical in a majority (>90%) of independent lineages.
source: The results demonstrated that only a relatively small fraction of protein sites (10–20%) are universally conserved, that is, they are identical in a majority (>90%) of independent lineages (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of site conservation across phylogenetically independent lineages, shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The observed long-term divergence limit is not primarily due to sets of universally conserved protein sites; instead, different sites contribute to the limit in independent phylogenetic lineages.
source: Therefore, the observed long-term divergence limit is not primarily due to sets of universally conserved protein sites; instead, different sites contribute to the limit in independent phylogenetic lineages.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the observation that universally conserved sites account for only a small fraction of overall sequence identity.

claim: Universally conserved sites account, on average, for only ~35% of the observed sequence identity at long divergence distances.
source: By comparing the fractions of universally conserved sites to the average sequence identity between distant orthologs (~40%, Figure 2a) we found that these sites account, on average, for only ~35% of the observed sequence identity at long divergence distances.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of universally conserved site fractions to overall sequence identity.

claim: Different protein families show different probability distributions of identical sites, likely due to diverse structural and functional requirements across protein families.
source: The analysis also revealed that different protein families show different probability distributions of identical sites (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). This is likely a consequence of diverse structural and functional requirements across protein families, leading to protein-family specific constraints on protein sites.
evidence: This claim is based on observed variation in site conservation patterns across protein families, with a speculative explanation.

claim: The long-term protein sequence identity between FolA orthologs is ~32%.
source: We selected FolA for the experiments due to its small size (159 amino acids) and essential role in the E. coli metabolism (Benkovic et al., 1988); also, the long-term protein sequence identity between FolA orthologs (~32%, see Figure 1a) is similar to other analyzed enzymes (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Sites with stronger fitness effects diverged more slowly.
source: Although, as expected, sites with stronger fitness effects diverged more slowly, our analysis revealed interesting differences in temporal divergence patterns for sites with small and large fitness effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of FolA divergence patterns grouped by fitness effects.

claim: For sites in the least deleterious fitness group, there was a substantial decrease (~10 fold) in mutual divergence rates after ~1.5 billion years of evolution.
source: For sites in the least deleterious fitness group (Figure 4a, blue) we observed, similar to the global sequence identity, a substantial decrease (~10 fold, see Equation 5 in Materials and methods) in mutual divergence rates after ~1.5 billion years of evolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of divergence patterns for sites with mild fitness effects, shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Even for FolA sites with mild fitness effects, sequence identity remains above 25% at long divergence distances.
source: Notably, even for FolA sites with mild fitness effects, sequence identity remains above 25% at long divergence distances.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Sites with the most deleterious mutations displayed a much slower, but approximately constant average divergence rate throughout evolutionary history.
source: In contrast to sites with mild fitness effects, sites with the most deleterious mutations (Figure 4a, black) displayed a much slower, but approximately constant average divergence rate throughout evolutionary history.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of divergence patterns for sites with large fitness effects, shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The divergence at sites with large fitness effects is not yet close to saturation.
source: This pattern suggests that, in contrast to divergence at sites with small fitness effects, the divergence at sites with large effects is not yet close to saturation.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the observation of constant divergence rates at sites with large fitness effects.

claim: The long-term divergence patterns were qualitatively similar between FolA and InfA proteins.
source: Consistent with the relatively higher level of sequence conservation of InfA, we observed lower average mutant growth rates and lower rates of sequence divergence in each fitness group. Nevertheless, the long-term divergence patterns were qualitatively similar between the two proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of divergence patterns between FolA and InfA shown in Figure 4.

claim: For both FolA and InfA, the probability that a protein site is identical at large divergence distances first increases approximately linearly with increasing average fitness effects, and then begins to saturate for sites with large (>30% growth rate decrease) fitness effects.
source: For both FolA and InfA, the probability that a protein site is identical at large divergence distances first increases, approximately linearly with increasing average fitness effects, and then begins to saturate for sites with large (>30% growth rate decrease) fitness effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The fitness effects at a protein site correlate with the site's conservation even after billions of years of evolution.
source: Thus, the fitness effects at a protein site correlate with the site's conservation even after billions of years of evolution.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the observed relationship between fitness effects and site conservation at long divergence times.

claim: The average root mean square deviation (RMSD) between C-alpha atoms of orthologous enzymes increases with divergence time.
source: This analysis demonstrated that the average root mean square deviation (RMSD) between C-alpha atoms of the orthologous enzymes increases (Spearman's r = 0.44, p-value<1e-20) with divergence time (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of orthologous enzymes shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The C-alpha RMSD between orthologs rarely increases beyond 3 Å, even at long evolutionary distances.
source: Nevertheless, the C-alpha RMSD between orthologs rarely increases beyond 3 Å, even at long evolutionary distances.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: There is a substantial decrease in the rate of structural divergence after ~1.5 billion years of divergent evolution.
source: Consistent with sequence evolution (Figure 1), we also observed a substantial decrease in the rate of structural divergence after ~1.5 billion years of divergent evolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Evolutionary rates of amino acid substitutions correlate with protein sites' spatial distance to catalytic residues.
source: It was previously demonstrated that evolutionary rates of amino acid substitutions correlate with protein sites' spatial distance to catalytic residues (Jack et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jack et al., 2016.

claim: Residues close to the active site were the most highly conserved.
source: Although, as expected, residues close to the active site were the most highly conserved (Jack et al., 2016; Halabi et al., 2009), even distant sites displayed a substantial divergence limit (~40%) at long evolutionary distances.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of site conservation as a function of distance to active site, shown in Figure 5b, and citations to previous work.

claim: Even distant sites from the active site displayed a substantial divergence limit (~40%) at long evolutionary distances.
source: Although, as expected, residues close to the active site were the most highly conserved (Jack et al., 2016; Halabi et al., 2009), even distant sites displayed a substantial divergence limit (~40%) at long evolutionary distances.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The spatial constraints required for specific molecular function usually propagate throughout the entire protein structure and significantly limit the long-term divergence even at sites distant from catalytic residues.
source: This result suggests that the spatial constraints required for specific molecular function usually propagate throughout the entire protein structure and significantly limit the long-term divergence even at sites distant from catalytic residues.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the observation that even distant sites show substantial conservation.

claim: Orthologs sharing only the first three EC digits have significantly lower long-term sequence identities (27% vs. 37% identity) compared to enzymes sharing all four EC digits.
source: This analysis revealed significantly lower long-term sequence identities (27% vs. 37% identity, Mann-Whitney p-value<10−20) and structural similarities (2.4 vs. 1.8 Å RMSD, P-value 2 × 10−18) between orthologs sharing only partial EC numbers.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of sequence identities between orthologs with different levels of functional conservation.

claim: Orthologs sharing only the first three EC digits have significantly lower structural similarities (2.4 vs. 1.8 Å RMSD) compared to enzymes sharing all four EC digits.
source: This analysis revealed significantly lower long-term sequence identities (27% vs. 37% identity, Mann-Whitney p-value<10−20) and structural similarities (2.4 vs. 1.8 Å RMSD, P-value 2 × 10−18) between orthologs sharing only partial EC numbers.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of structural similarities between orthologs with different levels of functional conservation.

claim: Orthologs sharing only the first three EC digits are still substantially more conserved, both in sequence and structure, than pairs of enzymes with the same structural fold but unrelated enzyme activities.
source: Notably, orthologs sharing only the first three EC digits are still substantially more conserved, both in sequence and structure (p-values<10−20), than pairs of enzymes with the same structural fold, but unrelated enzyme activities (i.e. enzymes sharing no digits in the EC classification) (Figure 6a and b, Dawson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 6a and b.

claim: Even at the same level of C-alpha RMSD divergence, orthologs sharing full EC numbers usually have higher levels of sequence identity compared to orthologous pairs with the same level of structural divergence but sharing only three EC digits.
source: Interestingly, we observed that even at the same level of C-alpha RMSD divergence, orthologs sharing full EC numbers usually have higher levels of sequence identity compared to orthologous pairs with the same level of structural divergence but sharing only three EC digits.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Conservation of molecular function constrains sequence divergence even beyond the requirement to maintain a specific spatial structure.
source: This result indicates that conservation of molecular function constrains sequence divergence even beyond the requirement to maintain a specific spatial structure.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the observation that sequence identity differs at the same structural divergence level depending on functional conservation.

claim: In contrast to proteins with the same fold, the requirement to strictly conserve the same molecular function significantly limits the long-term sequence and structural divergence of protein orthologs.
source: Our analysis demonstrates that, in contrast to proteins with the same fold (Rost, 1997), the requirement to strictly conserve the same molecular function significantly limits the long-term sequence and structural divergence of protein orthologs.
evidence: This claim summarizes a key finding of the study, supported by comparison to previous work on fold conservation.

claim: Ancient protein orthologs are still diverging from each other.
source: Although we confirmed the result by Povolotskaya and Kondrashov (2010) that ancient protein orthologs are still diverging from each other, our study reveals that the rate of this divergence becomes increasingly slow for orthologs that strictly conserve their function.
evidence: This claim confirms a previous finding by Povolotskaya and Kondrashov (2010).

claim: The rate of divergence becomes increasingly slow for orthologs that strictly conserve their function.
source: Although we confirmed the result by Povolotskaya and Kondrashov (2010) that ancient protein orthologs are still diverging from each other, our study reveals that the rate of this divergence becomes increasingly slow for orthologs that strictly conserve their function.
evidence: This claim is a key finding of the study, supported by analysis of divergence rates over time.

claim: Even a slight relaxation of functional specificity, for example from full to partial EC conservation, leads to substantially more pronounced long-term sequence and structural divergence.
source: Even a slight relaxation of functional specificity, for example from full to partial EC conservation (Figure 6a and b), leads to substantially more pronounced long-term sequence and structural divergence.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of divergence between orthologs with different levels of functional conservation, shown in Figure 6.

claim: A substantial sequence identity between homologous restriction endonucleases is usually limited to isoschizomers, that is, proteins specific to the same target DNA sequence.
source: Similarly, a substantial sequence identity between homologous restriction endonucleases is usually limited to isoschizomers, that is, proteins specific to the same target DNA sequence (Pingoud et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pingoud et al., 2014, providing an analogous example from restriction endonucleases.

claim: Proteins with the same molecular function usually conserve the identity of their chemical and biological substrates and interaction partners.
source: Proteins with the same molecular function usually conserve the identity of their chemical and biological substrates and interaction partners.
evidence: This claim is part of a mechanistic model explaining the observed divergence patterns.

claim: Conservation of substrates and interaction partners leads to functional pressure to closely preserve the spatial positions and dynamics of key protein residues necessary for efficient catalysis and function.
source: This conservation leads to functional pressure to closely preserve the spatial positions and dynamics of key protein residues necessary for efficient catalysis and function (Lehninger et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is part of a mechanistic model, supported by citation to biochemistry textbook.

claim: The requirement to continuously preserve structural properties and functional dynamics of key protein residues likely imposes a strict requirement to preserve the overall protein structure, in other words, structural optimality necessary for efficient and specific protein function.
source: In turn, the requirement to continuously preserve structural properties and functional dynamics of key protein residues likely imposes a strict requirement to preserve the overall protein structure, in other words, structural optimality necessary for efficient and specific protein function.
evidence: This claim is part of a mechanistic model explaining the observed constraints.

claim: The evolutionary pressure to preserve structural optimality (to within <3 Å C-alpha RMSD) required for a given molecular function leads to substantial levels of overall sequence conservation and the observed divergence limit.
source: The evolutionary pressure to preserve structural optimality (to within <3 Å C-alpha RMSD) required for a given molecular function leads, in agreement with the results by Chothia and Lesk (1986) and others (Gilson et al., 2017), to substantial levels of overall sequence conservation and the observed divergence limit.
evidence: This claim is part of a mechanistic model, supported by agreement with previous work.

claim: The observed conservation may reflect both the impact of amino acid substitutions on protein activity, due to changes in equilibrium positions and dynamics of protein residues, and on protein abundance, due to changes in overall protein stability.
source: We note that the observed conservation may reflect both the impact of amino acid substitutions on protein activity, due to changes in equilibrium positions and dynamics of protein residues, and on protein abundance, due to changes in overall protein stability (Bershtein et al., 2015; Adkar et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim acknowledges multiple potential mechanisms for conservation, supported by citations.

claim: Direct and comprehensive biochemical experiments demonstrated that the deleterious effects of mutations primarily arise from changes in specific protein activity rather than decreases in protein stability and cellular abundance.
source: Nevertheless, direct and comprehensive biochemical experiments demonstrated that the deleterious effects of mutations primarily arise from changes in specific protein activity rather than decreases in protein stability and cellular abundance (Firnberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Firnberg et al., 2016.

claim: Conservation of functional specificity imposes substantially more stringent long-term sequence constraints than simply conservation of protein folds and protein stability.
source: Our results support this model, demonstrating that conservation of functional specificity imposes substantially more stringent long-term sequence constraints than simply conservation of protein folds and protein stability.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of divergence limits for proteins with conserved function versus conserved fold.

claim: Maintaining stable folds does not constrain long-term divergence to more than 10-15% sequence identity, which is substantially less than the requirement for maintaining specific molecular functions (~40% sequence identity).
source: Indeed, while every folded protein should maintain its stability, our results demonstrate that maintaining stable folds does not constrain long-term divergence to more than 10-15% sequence identity, which is substantially less than the requirement for maintaining specific molecular functions (~40% sequence identity).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of divergence limits for fold conservation versus functional conservation.

claim: Only about a third of the sequence conservation between distant orthologs with the same molecular function can be attributed to universally conserved protein sites.
source: The presented results demonstrate that only about a third of the sequence conservation between distant orthologs with the same molecular function can be attributed to universally conserved protein sites, that is, sites occupied by identical amino acids in almost all lineages.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of universally conserved sites shown in Figure 3.

claim: Different protein sites are usually identical between orthologs from different lineages.
source: In contrast, we found that different protein sites are usually identical between orthologs from different lineages.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of site conservation across independent lineages.

claim: The finding that different sites are conserved in different lineages is likely due, at least in part, to the epistatic nature of protein sequence landscapes, where mutations that are neutral in one lineage are often prohibitively deleterious in another.
source: This result is likely due, at least in part, to the epistatic nature of protein sequence landscapes, where mutations that are neutral in one lineage are often prohibitively deleterious in another (Breen et al., 2012; Lunzer et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim provides a mechanistic explanation for lineage-specific conservation, supported by citations.

claim: The evolution of mitochondrial ribosomal proteins in eukaryotes provides an interesting example suggesting that orthologs' divergence can be substantially accelerated by co-evolution with their interaction partners or relaxation of selection pressures.
source: In the context of the aforementioned divergence model, the evolution of mitochondrial ribosomal proteins in eukaryotes (Figure 1—figure supplement 6) provides an interesting example, suggesting that orthologs' divergence can be substantially accelerated by co-evolution with their interaction partners or relaxation of selection pressures.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the observed differential divergence patterns in mitochondrial ribosomal proteins.

claim: During the first 1–2 billion years of divergence, substitutions at protein sites with mild fitness effects lead to a substantial (40–60%) decrease in sequence identity.
source: During the first 1–2 billion years of divergence, substitutions at protein sites with mild fitness effects lead to a substantial (40–60%) decrease in sequence identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of divergence patterns for sites with different fitness effects shown in Figure 4.

claim: After the first stage of divergence, divergence at sites with mild fitness effects effectively saturates.
source: After the first stage, divergence at these sites effectively saturates.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of divergence patterns shown in Figure 4.

claim: The saturation at sites with small fitness effects, combined with very slow divergence rate at sites with large fitness effects, leads to a substantially slower sequence and structural divergence during the second stage.
source: The saturation at sites with small fitness effects, combined with very slow divergence rate at sites with large fitness effects (Figure 4), leads to a substantially slower sequence and structural divergence during the second stage.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the observed divergence patterns at sites with different fitness effects.

claim: For the past billion years there has not been a substantial decrease in sequence and structural similarity between ancient orthologs with the same molecular function.
source: Interestingly, as a consequence of this slowdown, for the past billion years there has not been a substantial decrease in sequence and structural similarity between ancient orthologs with the same molecular function.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the observed slowdown in divergence rates.
